name: Offline
oneLine: Stalls, pop-ups, and door-to-door: the fastest way to your first real sale
tagline: Stalls, pop-ups, and door-to-door: the fastest way to your first real sale
why: Offline is usually the fastest channel to first revenue because it removes every friction point of an online sale, no waiting for a click, no trust to build from scratch with a stranger on the internet. You're in front of a real person, with a real product, and a UPI QR code. It's also your best source of unfiltered feedback: you'll know within 30 seconds if your pitch, price, or product isn't landing.
how: Set up a small, visual stall (table, banner, product display) or go door-to-door with a sample kit. Lead with a physical demo, not a pitch, let people touch or try the product, use a short hook line, and close with a bundle or urgency offer. Accept payment via a UPI QR code tested beforehand, or cash.
when: High-footfall windows, not just any free time, hostel entrances at meal times, the 10 minutes between lecture blocks, weekend campus events, and any college fest or society event. Door-to-door works best early evening on weekdays, once people are back from class.
where: Anywhere your target customer already gathers in numbers, hostel common areas, the walkway outside popular lecture halls, campus food courts, society or club events, local weekend markets open to outside vendors, apartments, etc.
whatYouNeed: A UPI QR code tested with a real transaction, price signage, 15-20 units of visible (unboxed) stock, a table or stand if available, a rehearsed hook line, inventory & lots of energy!
gettingStarted: A UPI QR code that works, tested with a real ₹10 transaction
Visible price signage: people should know what they're looking at from 6 feet away (depending on your product)
15-20 units of stock, displayed, not boxed
One clear hook line you can say in under 10 seconds
A shortlist of 3 locations, ranked by expected footfall

playbook.title: Pick your spot like it's the only decision that matters
playbook.body: Because it is. High-footfall plus a captive, relevant audience beats a “nice” location every time.

playbook.title: Set up in under 10 minutes
playbook.body: A banner, a price list, and product displayed so people can touch it. Nothing stays in boxes.

playbook.title: Open with a hook, not a pitch
playbook.body: “Try this for free” or “This is the softest sock you'll ever wear, 10 seconds” beats “Hi, we're a D2C brand…” every time.

playbook.title: Let them touch, smell, try
playbook.body: Physical products sell themselves once someone's holding them, your job is just to get the product into their hands.

playbook.title: Handle the price objection before they raise it
playbook.body: If you're not the cheapest, say why in one line: “₹50 more, but it lasts three times as long.”

playbook.title: Always closing with a bundle
playbook.body: “Buy 2, get 10% off” converts more browsers than a flat single-unit price.

playbook.title: Capture the contact
playbook.body: Every buyer, and every serious browser, should leave a WhatsApp number or Instagram follow behind, this is how you retarget them for round two.

stuck.symptom: Nobody's stopping at my stall
stuck.fix: Move your best-seller to the very front, add a “FREE TRY” sign, or hand samples to people walking past instead of waiting for them to approach.

stuck.symptom: People stop, look, and walk away
stuck.fix: Your hook line is probably too generic. Say the one specific thing that makes your product different, out loud, in the first 5 seconds.

stuck.symptom: They love it but don't buy
stuck.fix: Add urgency (“only here today”) or a bundle discount, indecision usually means the price-to-value gap isn't closed yet, not that they don't want it.

stuck.symptom: Sales are one-offs, no repeats
stuck.fix: You're not capturing contacts. Start a simple “spin the wheel for 10% off” in exchange for a phone number.

goodLooksLike: 1 in every 5-8 people who stop at your stall should convert. If you're below that, it's a pitch or price problem, not a footfall problem.
avoid: Setting up somewhere “nice” instead of somewhere busy
Standing behind the stall instead of in front of it, waving people down
Quoting price before demonstrating value
Packing up early because “it's slow”: the last hour of any event is often the best

name: Online Organic
oneLine: Instagram, website, and content: your cheapest, most compounding channel, if you're consistent
tagline: Instagram, website, and content: your cheapest, most compounding channel, if you're consistent
why: Every post, reel, and story is a free, permanent asset that keeps working after you've moved on. Unlike a stall, online organic scales without you being physically present, but it rewards consistency and punishes half-effort content far more visibly than offline does.
how: Post consistently across four content buckets (product-in-use, behind-the-scenes, social proof, value/entertainment), lead with Reels, use Stories to sell directly to your warmest audience, and respond to every DM and comment fast. Your website should convert whatever your content brings in.
when: Post daily if you can manage it, every other day at minimum, both the algorithm and your audience punish long gaps. Test early morning (before class) and evening (post-dinner scrolling) to see what your specific audience responds to.
where: Instagram is your primary platform for a campus-and-family D2C audience. Your website is where the purchase happens. WhatsApp Status and Broadcast is a strong secondary channel for a smaller, warmer audience, classmates, family, existing customers.
whatYouNeed: A content calendar at least 2 weeks out, a phone camera and a basic editing app, a few consistent props or backgrounds, a working store link in your bio, and a habit of checking DMs multiple times a day.
gettingStarted: Instagram bio: one line on what you sell, a link to your store, and your best product photo pinned
9-12 grid posts before you start posting daily, never launch with an empty grid
A content calendar for the next 2 weeks, planned in one sitting
Your website's “Buy Now” button tested end-to-end, including payment

playbook.title: Post in four buckets, on rotation
playbook.body: Product-in-use, behind-the-scenes, social proof (a customer's reaction or review), and value/entertainment (a tip or trend related to your category).

playbook.title: Reels first, always
playbook.body: On a new account, Reels reach far beyond your followers; static posts mostly don't. Aim for 3-4 Reels a week minimum.

playbook.title: Use Stories to sell directly
playbook.body: Polls (“which colour next?”), countdowns to a drop, and a direct “swipe up to buy”, Stories convert your warmest audience, the people who already follow you.

playbook.title: Answer every DM and comment within the hour
playbook.body: Early-stage accounts live or die on responsiveness, a fast reply to “is this available in blue?” is often the entire sales conversation.

playbook.title: Make your website do the convincing your salesperson can't
playbook.body: Multiple product photos, a clear price, 2-3 real reviews, and a checkout under 60 seconds.

playbook.title: Track what's actually working
playbook.body: Which single post drove the most profile visits or DMs? Do more of exactly that, not more of “content” in general.

faqs.q: How many followers do I actually need before this works?
faqs.a: Fewer than you think: you need relevant reach, not scale. 200 highly relevant followers (classmates, hostel mates) can outsell 2,000 random ones.

faqs.q: Should the account feel personal or more corporate?
faqs.a: Lean personal, especially early. People buy from people at this stage, show your face and process, not just product shots.

faqs.q: I'm getting views but the wrong audience. What's wrong?
faqs.a: Check your hashtags and topics: you may be reaching a broad, unrelated audience. Narrow your hashtags to your specific niche and location.

faqs.q: Is it worth boosting a post before I have ad budget?
faqs.a: Not usually. Save any small budget for a proper Performance Marketing test instead, a one-off boosted post rarely builds anything lasting.

faqs.q: How do I know if it's my content or my website that's the problem?
faqs.a: Compare Instagram profile visits to actual website visits and sales. A gap between profile visits and site clicks means your bio/CTA is the issue; a gap between site visits and sales means your website is.

stuck.symptom: Posts get views but no engagement
stuck.fix: Your caption probably has no question or CTA. End every post with something that invites a reply.

stuck.symptom: Followers growing, but no sales
stuck.fix: Check your bio link actually goes to a working store, and that your Stories are asking people to buy, followers don't convert on their own.

stuck.symptom: Website traffic but no checkout completions
stuck.fix: Get a friend to buy something right now and time it. Over 90 seconds, or asking for information it doesn't need, is your leak.

stuck.symptom: I don't know what to post
stuck.fix: Film 5 things today: you unboxing your own product, a customer using it, your workspace, a before/after, and you answering a common question. That's a week of content.

goodLooksLike: Aim for at least 1 DM inquiry per 3 Reels once you're past your first 15-20 posts, and a website conversion rate of 1-2% is a reasonable early target.
avoid: Posting only product photos with no faces or story
Going quiet for more than 2-3 days once you've started
A bio link that goes to Instagram itself instead of your store
Deleting posts that “didn't do well” instead of learning why

name: Influencer Marketing
oneLine: Borrowed trust, borrowed audience: if you pick the right partner
tagline: Borrowed trust, borrowed audience: if you pick the right partner
why: A stranger trusts a creator they already follow more than they trust your brand-new account. Influencer marketing is really just renting that trust for a short campaign, and at the nano/micro level (1K-20K followers), it's cheap or free, and often more effective per rupee than paid ads.
how: Shortlist relevant creators, send a short and specific ask (barter or paid), give a loose creative brief, attach a trackable code or link, and follow up once if you don't hear back.
when: Reach out at least 1-2 weeks before you need content live, creators need time to film, edit, and post, and content performs best timed around a specific moment: a launch, a discount window, or an event.
where: Instagram first, but also consider YouTube Shorts creators and fellow students with a strong personal following, campus micro-influencers often convert better than generic lifestyle accounts.
whatYouNeed: A shortlist of 15-20 names, a one-line pitch message, product to send for barter, a trackable discount code per creator, and a simple tracker logging who you've contacted, their response, and what they posted.
gettingStarted: A shortlist of 15-20 nano/micro creators in your category or campus network
A simple, specific outreach message template
A unique discount code or trackable link per creator, so you know what's actually working
Clarity on barter vs. paid before you reach out

playbook.title: Prioritize relevance over reach
playbook.body: A 3,000-follower creator whose entire audience is your target customer beats a 30,000-follower generalist every time.

playbook.title: Start with campus and hyperlocal creators
playbook.body: They're easier to reach, cheaper (often barter-only), and their audience overlaps almost exactly with your early buyers.

playbook.title: Send a specific, short ask
playbook.body: Not “we'd love to collaborate”: instead: “We'll send you [product] to keep, and we'd love one Reel/Story showing how you use it. Interested?”

playbook.title: Give a loose brief, not a script
playbook.body: Creators know their audience better than you do, tell them the 1-2 things that must come across, and let them make it their own.

playbook.title: Always attach a trackable code or link
playbook.body: Without this, you can't tell a campaign that worked from one that didn't, and you'll repeat the wrong ones.

playbook.title: Follow up once, politely, after 3-4 days of silence
playbook.body: Most non-responses are just a full inbox, not a no.

faqs.q: Barter or pay: which should I choose first?
faqs.a: Start with barter for nano/campus creators: most will say yes for a free product plus visibility. Save paid deals for creators who specifically ask, or who clearly deliver strong results.

faqs.q: A creator wants a large payment upfront, what do I do?
faqs.a: Politely decline and offer a smaller barter test first to prove fit before any paid commitment. Don't pay a large amount for an unproven relationship.

faqs.q: How do I know if their content actually worked?
faqs.a: Look at three things: their unique code's redemptions, click-throughs on their link (if trackable), and any comment/DM spike right after they posted.

faqs.q: Should I ask for exclusivity from a creator?
faqs.a: Not at this stage: you're not paying enough to reasonably ask for it. Focus on getting one good collaboration done well instead.

faqs.q: Their content doesn't feel “on brand”: is that a problem?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Their authentic voice is often exactly what makes it work, a tight brief helps, but don't over-correct into something generic.

stuck.symptom: Creators aren't replying
stuck.fix: Go smaller and more local: a 500-follower classmate with an engaged niche account will often say yes when a 20K-follower stranger won't.

stuck.symptom: They posted, but no one used the code
stuck.fix: The CTA in their post was probably vague. Ask them to say the code out loud in the video and pin it in the caption.

stuck.symptom: Good engagement, but no sales
stuck.fix: Check if the discount is actually compelling enough to move someone from “interested” to “buying today”, 10% often isn't enough for a first-time buyer.

stuck.symptom: I don't know who to approach
stuck.fix: Search hashtags and locations relevant to your product on Instagram, and look at who's already engaging with brands like yours.

goodLooksLike: For nano/micro creators, a 2-5% conversion rate on their unique code is a healthy benchmark for a first campaign.
avoid: Chasing follower count instead of engagement or relevance
No written brief at all: leads to off-brand content
Paying full rate before testing with a barter deal first
Forgetting to repost their content to your own page

name: Performance Marketing
oneLine: Paid ads: the fastest way to burn ₹5,000 and learn nothing, unless you do this in order
tagline: Paid ads: the fastest way to burn ₹5,000 and learn nothing, unless you do this in order
why: Paid ads are the only channel where you can buy attention on demand, targeted precisely to people who look like your best customers, but they're also the channel most likely to waste your capital if you skip the fundamentals. Tracking and a working funnel have to exist before a single rupee of spend.
how: Install tracking first, build a specific landing page, test 3 creatives on a small budget, read your funnel numbers in order (CTR, then landing page conversion, then ROAS), then kill or scale based on what the data says.
when: Start testing once you have a working store and at least a few organic sales or reviews as social proof. Give any test 2-3 days minimum before judging it, the algorithm needs time to learn.
where: Meta (Instagram + Facebook) is usually the first stop for a visual D2C product, cheaper to start and easier to test creative on. Google is better once you have clear search demand for your specific product category.
whatYouNeed: Meta Pixel installed and confirmed firing, a dedicated landing page, 3 ad creatives, a small daily test budget (₹500-1,000/day), and a habit of checking performance daily, not hourly.
gettingStarted: Meta Pixel and/or Google Analytics installed and confirmed firing on your website
A landing page, not just your homepage, that matches exactly what the ad promises
3 different ad creatives ready to test against each other
A small test budget agreed in advance, ₹500-1,000/day is enough to learn

playbook.title: Test before you scale
playbook.body: Run all 3 creatives to a small, broad-ish audience for 2-3 days before touching the budget slider.

playbook.title: Read three numbers, in this order
playbook.body: CTR (are people interested enough to click?), then landing page conversion rate (does the page deliver?), then ROAS (does the math work?). A failure at any stage tells you exactly where to fix.

playbook.title: Kill fast, scale slower
playbook.body: Cut a creative that's clearly underperforming after ~₹300-500 of spend. When something works, scale the budget by 20-30% at a time, not by doubling overnight.

playbook.title: Match your ad's promise to your landing page's headline
playbook.body: If the ad says “40% off,” the landing page should say that in the first line the visitor sees.

playbook.title: Watch for ad fatigue
playbook.body: If a winning ad's performance drops after a week or two, it's been seen too many times by the same people, refresh the creative, don't kill the audience.

playbook.title: Retarget people who almost bought
playbook.body: Anyone who visited your product page but didn't purchase is your cheapest, highest-intent audience for a second ad.

faqs.q: How much should I spend to get useful data?
faqs.a: Budget at least ₹1,500-2,000 total per creative before making a real call, spending ₹200 and giving up tells you almost nothing.
Don't expect 3+ in week one. Anything above 1.5-2 is worth building on; below 1 across a real test budget usually means targeting, creative, or the page needs to change.

faqs.q: Can I run this myself, or do I need a mentor to manage it?
faqs.a: You can run this yourself: that's the point of the program. Use WS11 (Performance Marketing workshop) and this guide as your baseline, then practice.

faqs.q: What if I don't have ₹500/day to spend?
faqs.a: Start smaller: even ₹200-300/day is enough to learn directional signals, like which creative gets more clicks, even without full conversion volume yet.

faqs.q: My ROAS looks great but I'm still short on cash, why?
faqs.a: ROAS measures revenue against ad spend only, not your total costs. Check the Revenue & Expenses section, a “great” ROAS can still hide a thin overall margin.

stuck.symptom: High CTR, but nobody buys
stuck.fix: The problem is your landing page or price, not your ad. Check load speed, and make sure the price and value are obvious in the first 5 seconds.

stuck.symptom: Nobody's clicking at all
stuck.fix: Your creative isn't stopping the scroll: try a UGC-style video over a polished product shot; it usually outperforms for cold audiences.

stuck.symptom: Spend is going up, ROAS is going down
stuck.fix: You're probably seeing ad fatigue or audience saturation, refresh the creative or widen the audience slightly.

stuck.symptom: I don't know if I'm ready to spend more
stuck.fix: You're ready to scale only once one creative has a proven ROAS above 2 across at least ₹1,500-2,000 of spend, not before.

goodLooksLike: Aim for a ROAS of 3+ before scaling meaningfully; anything above 2 in week one is a promising early signal, not yet a scale signal.
avoid: Spending before the Pixel/tracking is confirmed working
Sending ad traffic to your homepage instead of a specific product page
Scaling budget on day one because “it seemed to work”
Judging a campaign on likes or reach instead of ROAS

name: B2B
oneLine: Bulk and institutional sales: fewer conversations, bigger tickets
tagline: Bulk and institutional sales: fewer conversations, bigger tickets
why: One good B2B deal can be worth 50-100 individual D2C sales in a single conversation. For a time-constrained challenge, a handful of well-run B2B relationships can move your revenue number more than weeks of one-at-a-time selling, and hostels, cafes, gyms, and offices are constantly buying things in bulk anyway.
how: Build a warm path wherever possible, lead with their problem, bring a sample, propose a small pilot order rather than a big first ask, follow up relentlessly, and turn every pilot into a bigger repeat order conversation.
when: Start by Phase 2 at the latest, B2B sales cycles take longer than a week even for a small deal. Don't wait until you're behind on revenue to start; by then you won't have time for the follow-up this channel needs.
where: Gyms near campus, corporate HR/admin teams via warm intros, boutique local retailers, and your own or classmates' family businesses, the best first targets are places you already have some kind of “in.”
whatYouNeed: A shortlist of 15-20 targets, a 1-2 page pitch deck, a small sample kit, clear bulk pricing tiers decided in advance, and a simple tracker for who you've contacted and your last follow-up date.
gettingStarted: A shortlist of 15-20 targets: Corporate HR/admin teams, boutique retailers, any businesses.
A 1-2 page pitch deck: what you sell, why it's good for them, pricing at volume
A small sample kit ready to hand over or send
Clarity on your bulk pricing tiers before anyone asks

playbook.title: Build a warm path wherever possible
playbook.body: A cold LinkedIn message works, but an introduction from a friend, family member, or professor gets you a meeting 3x faster.

playbook.title: Lead with their problem, not your product
playbook.body: A gym doesn't want “premium socks”: it wants “a member gift that doesn't cost staff time to source.” Frame around what they need.

playbook.title: Bring, or send, a physical sample
playbook.body: B2B buyers, like anyone else, decide faster once they can hold the product.

playbook.title: Propose a small pilot, not a huge first order
playbook.body: “Let's start with 25 units and see how they move” is a much easier yes than asking for a 200-unit commitment upfront.

playbook.title: Make the follow-up your job, not theirs
playbook.body: Most B2B deals die from silence, not rejection, follow up every 3-4 days until you get a real yes or no.

playbook.title: Turn every pilot into a repeat order conversation
playbook.body: The moment a pilot sells through, go back and ask for the next, bigger order, don't wait for them to come back to you.

faqs.q: How much should I discount for bulk orders?
faqs.a: Set 2-3 clear pricing tiers in advance (e.g. 10% off at 25+ units, 15% off at 50+) so you're never negotiating on the spot, know your floor margin before you walk in.

faqs.q: What if they ask for a much bigger order than I can fulfill?
faqs.a: Be honest about your production capacity and propose a phased delivery, a smaller first batch now, the rest to follow, rather than overpromising.

faqs.q: I got a verbal yes but no payment yet, does that count?
faqs.a: Not until there's a confirmed order and at least a partial payment or advance. Verbal interest isn't revenue, and treating it as such will throw off your milestone tracking.

faqs.q: How many “no”s should I expect before a “yes”?
faqs.a: Plan for it: a realistic funnel is roughly 15-20 outreaches to 2-3 closed pilots. A string of no's early on is normal, not a signal to stop.

stuck.symptom: No one's replying to outreach
stuck.fix: Switch from cold email/LinkedIn to WhatsApp or an in-person drop-in with a sample, B2B here is often won in person, not in an inbox.

stuck.symptom: I get meetings, but no one commits
stuck.fix: You're probably asking for too big a first order. Shrink the task to a small pilot with no long-term commitment.

stuck.symptom: They say yes but go quiet on payment/logistics
stuck.fix: Get a UPI advance or confirmed order in writing at the meeting itself, not “let's finalize later.”

stuck.symptom: I don't know who to approach
stuck.fix: Start with places you already have a natural way in, your own hostel, your professor's department, a friend's family business.

goodLooksLike: A realistic B2B funnel here is roughly 15-20 outreaches → 5-8 meetings → 2-3 closed pilots. If you're far below that, the issue is usually the ask size or follow-up discipline, not the product.
avoid: Cold-emailing 50 places and following up with none of them
Asking for a large order before you've proven a small one
Undercutting your own margin just to close a first deal
Treating a single “yes” as the finish line instead of the start of a repeat relationship
